units.t: The Sketchbook and the Creative Process

learn: A sketchbook is an artist's notebook for ideas, practice and experiments.
Leonardo da Vinci filled thousands of notebook pages with drawings and notes.
Mistakes in a sketchbook are part of learning.
lessons.try: Fill one sketchbook page a day for a week.

learn: The creative process: inspire, brainstorm, plan, create, reflect and revise.
Thumbnail sketches are small quick drafts of composition ideas.
Artists often make several versions before the final piece.
check: The last stage of the process includes...
lessons.try: Make six thumbnail sketches for one idea.

learn: Inspiration comes from nature, memories, music, stories and other art.
Artists keep reference photos and collections.
Combine ideas in surprising ways.
check: Combining ideas in new ways is...
lessons.try: Make a mood board of images that inspire you.

learn: Divide your picture into a 3-by-3 grid.
Place important subjects on the lines or where they cross.
This often creates more interesting compositions than centring.
check: The rule of thirds uses a ___ grid.
The rule of thirds often makes images...
lessons.try: Take three photos using the rule of thirds.

learn: Leading lines guide the viewer's eye: roads, rivers, fences.
A focal point is where the eye goes first.
Contrast, colour and placement create focal points.
lessons.try: Draw a landscape with a road that leads to a focal point.

learn: Framing uses elements in the scene (doorways, branches) to surround the subject.
Cropping removes distracting parts.
Viewfinders (a cardboard window) help choose a composition.
check: A doorway around a subject is...
lessons.try: Make a cardboard viewfinder and find three compositions in your room.

learn: The eyes sit halfway down the head.
The bottom of the nose is halfway between the eyes and chin; the mouth is a third of the way from nose to chin.
The space between the eyes is about one eye-width.
check: The space between the eyes is about...
The ears line up roughly between the...
lessons.try: Draw a face using a proportion guide.

learn: Use a mirror and look carefully.
Rembrandt painted around 80 self-portraits over his life.
Self-portraits can show personality, mood and identity.
check: The best tool for a self-portrait is a...
lessons.try: Draw a self-portrait from a mirror.

learn: Expressions change the eyebrows, eyes and mouth.
A profile is a side view of the face.
Exaggerating features carefully creates caricature.
check: A side view of a face is a...
lessons.try: Draw the same face with three expressions.

learn: Landscapes are often arranged in three planes: foreground, middle ground and background.
Overlapping and size change show depth.
The horizon line marks where sky meets land.
check: The part closest to the viewer is the...
Where sky meets land is the...
lessons.try: Sketch a landscape with clear foreground, middle ground and background.

learn: Distant objects are lighter, bluer and less detailed.
Mix a little blue and white into distant colours.
Keep strong contrast and detail in the foreground.
lessons.try: Paint three hills, each lighter and bluer.

learn: J. M. W. Turner painted dramatic light and weather.
John Constable painted the English countryside realistically.
The Hudson River School painted American wilderness in the 1800s.
lessons.try: Compare a Turner and a Constable painting.

learn: Watercolour is transparent; light colours go first and white comes from the paper.
Wet-on-wet creates soft blends; wet-on-dry creates crisp edges.
Salt and lifting with a tissue create textures.
lessons.try: Make a chart of five watercolour techniques.

learn: Acrylic is opaque and dries quickly; it can be layered.
Tempera is a bright, opaque school paint.
Brushes: flat for broad strokes, round for detail.
lessons.try: Paint a still life in acrylic using layers.

learn: Brushstrokes can be smooth or visible and expressive.
Impasto is thick paint that stands up from the surface.
Van Gogh's swirling brushwork adds energy.
lessons.try: Paint the same tree with smooth and expressive brushstrokes.

learn: Mixed media combines different materials in one artwork.
Examples: paint with paper, ink with fabric, drawing with photographs.
Mixed media encourages experimentation.
lessons.try: Make a small artwork using at least three materials.

learn: Collage glues pieces of paper, fabric or photos onto a surface.
Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque used collage in the early 1900s.
Henri Matisse made cut-paper collages late in his life.
lessons.try: Make a cut-paper collage inspired by Matisse.

learn: Layer transparent and opaque materials for depth.
Add texture with fabric, tissue paper or modelling paste.
Plan layers from back to front.
lessons.try: Make a layered landscape with tissue paper.

learn: Graphic design communicates ideas visually: posters, logos, packaging and websites.
Good design is clear, purposeful and attractive.
Designers think about the audience.
lessons.try: Collect three examples of graphic design you see daily.

learn: Typography is the art of arranging type (letters).
Serif fonts have small strokes at the ends; sans-serif fonts don't.
Hierarchy uses size and weight to show what to read first.
lessons.try: Design a poster with clear typographic hierarchy.

learn: Logos are simple, memorable symbols.
Posters combine image, text and colour to deliver a message quickly.
Limit fonts and colours for clarity.
lessons.try: Design a logo for a club.

units.t: Art Movements: Impressionism to Modern Art

learn: Impressionists like Claude Monet painted light outdoors with quick brushstrokes (1870s).
Post-Impressionists like Van Gogh, Cézanne and Georges Seurat added structure and emotion.
Seurat's pointillism used tiny dots of colour.
lessons.try: Paint a small scene using pointillism.

learn: Expressionists used bold colour and distortion to show emotion: Edvard Munch's "The Scream" (1893).
Cubists like Picasso and Braque broke objects into geometric shapes from many viewpoints.
Both moved away from realism.
lessons.try: Draw a cubist portrait of a friend.

learn: Abstract art uses shapes, colours and lines without depicting real objects: Wassily Kandinsky.
Surrealism painted dreamlike, impossible scenes.
Piet Mondrian used grids of primary colours.
lessons.try: Make an abstract painting inspired by music.

learn: Relief sculpture projects from a flat background.
Low relief (bas-relief) is shallow; high relief stands out more.
Coins and building friezes are examples.
lessons.try: Make a low-relief sculpture in clay or foil.

learn: Assemblage builds sculpture from found objects.
Louise Nevelson painted boxes of found wood a single colour.
Objects take on new meaning in art.
lessons.try: Build an assemblage from recycled objects, painted one colour.

learn: Kinetic sculpture moves.
Alexander Calder invented the mobile, a hanging balanced sculpture.
Balance and weight are key to mobiles.
lessons.try: Make a simple mobile from wire and card.

learn: Artists use their work to raise awareness and inspire change.
Posters, murals and photography have supported causes like conservation and civil rights.
Art can communicate across languages.
check: Art with a message aims to...
lessons.try: Discuss a work of art that carries a message.

learn: Murals are large paintings on walls.
Diego Rivera painted murals about workers and Mexican history.
Public art belongs to the whole community.
lessons.try: Design a mural for your school.

learn: Choose an issue you care about.
Plan symbols, colours and text that communicate clearly.
Present your work with an artist statement.
check: Start by choosing an issue you...
lessons.try: Create and present an artwork about an issue important to you.
